title: Ang 691–695: the Bhagats' aartis
tomorrow: can the bravest person in the room admit they're scared?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 684: why search the forest, when the One lives within, like fragrance in a flower. Within. Today the search gets very ordinary.

Somewhere in your notes app there's probably a grocery list: lentils, flour, oil, the thing you forgot last time. Turn to ang 695 of the Guru Granth Sahib and there's nearly that list, inside a hymn. Dhanna, a farmer in tradition, sings to God, and asks for lentils, flour and ghee. Then shoes, good clothes, grain, a cow, a fine horse. In scripture. So here's the puzzle: why does a holy book keep a shopping list?
screen: `A GROCERY LIST IN YOUR PHONE.` → `LENTILS, FLOUR AND GHEE.` → `WHY KEEP A SHOPPING LIST?`

segments.voice: These pages close Dhanasri with the Bhagats, saints from outside the line of the Gurus: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and others. Several of them sing an aarti, the song of worship sung as lamps are waved. A few days ago, Guru Nanak made the whole sky the aarti platter. Here the Bhagats bring it close. Ravidas, on ang 694: your Name is my aarti and my bath. Sain, a barber in tradition: lamps, incense and ghee for the aarti; I'm a sacrifice to you. Pipa, a king in tradition who gave up his throne: the body itself is the temple, the god and the pilgrim; whatever is in the universe is in the body, and whoever searches finds it. Then Dhanna. Lord, this is your aarti; you set right the affairs of those who worship you. And then the list, so that, as he says, the heart stays glad. So, the puzzle. The Granth doesn't keep Dhanna's list by accident. It keeps it beside Ravidas and Pipa, as an aarti in its own right. Worship doesn't have to sound grand. A farmer's real needs, said straight to God, count. Sikhs still pray that way: Ardas, the standing prayer, can name a meal, a journey, someone who's ill. Plain prayers.
screen: `THE BHAGATS CLOSE DHANASRI.` · `YOUR NAME IS MY AARTI.` · `THE BODY IS THE TEMPLE.` · `DHANNA'S LIST, KEPT ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `PLAIN PRAYERS.`

segments.voice: Say one plain need out loud, in ordinary words, the way Dhanna did: a good night's sleep, the rent, a friend who feels better soon. If you pray, that's a prayer; if not, it's still worth hearing yourself say it. Then let the sit hold the quiet that comes after.
Ang 691. Where the Bhagats' hymns in Dhanasri begin, ending in aartis: Ravidas, Sain, Pipa, and Dhanna's plain list.
Plain prayers: an aarti can be lentils and ghee, said straight, with a glad heart. That's day fifteen twenty-eight, and that's the list.

howItsDone: The Bhagats' aartis, among them Ravidas's 'your Name is my aarti' and Sain's, are sung in many gurdwaras in the evening, and Sikhs' Ardas often names ordinary needs and occasions.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape puzzle (why does scripture keep a shopping list?). Simran arc: wedding shopping with Bebe.
Confirm the Bhagats' Dhanasri hymns begin on ang 691, and the angs given: Ravidas's 'naam tero aaratee' (694); Sain, Pipa and Dhanna (695).

Dhanna's list paraphrased from 'daal seedhaa maagau gheeo… panneeaa chhaadan neekaa… anaaj magau sat seekaa… gaoo bhais… ik taajan turee changeree'; the line about a good wife was left out of the voice for brevity. Confirm.
Occupations (Dhanna a farmer, Sain a barber, Pipa a king who renounced his throne) are given as tradition. Confirm.

The reading that the Granth keeps Dhanna's list as an aarti 'in its own right' is the lesson's framing; Sikh commentators also read Dhanna's requests as the needs of a householder who stays devoted. Confirm fair.
Ardas naming ordinary occasions (a meal, a journey, someone ill) is described, not quoted. Confirm.
